item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-04-cn2d7912-读书只读到初中毕业-他把吹风机做到了全球销量第一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-04-cn2d7912-读书只读到初中毕业-他把吹风机做到了全球销量第一/
item.description: He built manned flying vehicles and electric scooters, twice burning through borrowed millions—but by teaching himself brushless motor technology, he priced a hair dryer at one-fifth of Dyson's and made it a global sales leader.
item.content:encoded:
He built manned flying vehicles and electric scooters, twice burning through borrowed millions—but by teaching himself brushless motor technology, he priced a hair dryer at one-fifth of Dyson's and made it a global sales leader.

A self-taught founder who never finished high school hit nearly every possible pitfall before finding his footing—his mistakes are more instructive than his wins.

12:09 Grades wounded him, but poverty and bullying did not
Trash-picking as a child, bullied in school as an outsider and poor student, always among the shortest kids in gym class—none of it left psychological scars. The one real wound: poor grades and teacher criticism. His temperament is ‘大条’ (thick-skinned)—he forgets stress easily. This early resilience explains how he could restart after multiple bankruptcies. The foundation was already there from childhood.

13:10 Yahoo's homepage hit him like science fiction
In 2003 he booted a second-hand computer and saw the Yahoo homepage—the shock of ‘all the world's information displayed in one place’ felt ‘特别科幻’. At 13,000 yuan per year, he enrolled in a no-credential computer training school, a major family expense. When they nominated a class leader, he volunteered—his first time building confidence by knowing more than his peers. Before this moment he was extremely withdrawn, afraid even to talk to strangers.

44:27 He burned millions on a manned flying machine—because scaling a drone looked simple
Around age 25, after selling his Taobao shop, he decided to build a hexacopter he could ride in. His reasoning: ‘I played with drones, so this is just putting a drone scaled up.’ The team scrounged factories and recruited grad students. The result: 20 minutes of flight time, poor reliability, millions in personal funds burned, funding pitches sent to VCs that all disappeared. He compares it to Li Shufu's line about cars—‘just a sofa with wheels’—which the entire country mocked, but which led to a massive business. Fearless ignorance is sometimes where boldness starts.

1:00:33 He sold scooters to one American buyer who hit $1 billion valuation
After the flying machine failed, the team borrowed over 3 million yuan for a second-generation electric scooter, mortgaging house and car. They built the product but lacked manufacturing capacity and brand channels, so they licensed it exclusively to an American buyer. That buyer took this single product to the US, registered a company, raised funding, and eventually achieved a peak valuation of $1 billion. Looking back, Ye realized it wasn't betrayal—he had zero business and fundraising skills at the time. He should have earned that value himself.

1:17:44 Two years to get a brushless motor right—and he rewrote it halfway through
When designing Laifen's first hair dryer motor, he started with an outer rotor, then quickly realized high-speed motors need inner rotors: ‘many designs were completely wrong’. Operating at 110,000 rpm, 300+ volts, the motor seized on the bearing. Chinese bearing manufacturers couldn't solve it; the core patents were locked by a Japanese company. Only through a buyer's supplier could he find a solution. What was supposed to take one year took two. His relationship with his business partner deteriorated; they split after launch.

1:19:46 Great products do not make great businesses
He reviewed why early fundraising failed: strong product instincts, but business logic full of holes—VCs saw through it instantly. His conclusion: product-driven companies succeed far less often than those run by strategists. Jobs is rare precisely because he was both a genius product manager and a capable CEO—that combination almost never appears in business history. Most founders who are strong only at product pay a steep price learning the business side. Ye paid it too.

1:34:54 Two casual videos went viral—and sales finally took off
After launch, sales were sluggish for four or five months. The turning point arrived by accident: two low-cost videos. One was a KOL explaining the product details. The other was him sitting in on a talk with investor Wang Huiwen (王慧文)—captured on camera, both men bald, talking sharp and direct. The clip spread everywhere: 200 million views globally. Comment sections identified him: ‘this bald head is Laifen's Ye.’ In the first few hours after posting, likes climbed from 10,000 to 200,000; the team watched the counter refresh in shock.

2:33:30 Accused of copying Dyson—he chose silence over the truth
When Laifen launched a razor, outcry erupted: it copied Dyson's design. The timeline proved him innocent—his patent was filed first, the launch gap was only 28 days (impossible to copy), his evidence chain was complete. Yet Ye decided not to defend publicly. His reasoning: ‘in marketing and PR, perception beats truth. If enough people believe you copied, there's no counter-narrative, and you stay silent—everyone concludes you copied.’ He admits not defending cost him. But if it happens twice or three times, ‘I might never wash it clean for the rest of my life’—so he accepted the loss to avoid compounding damage.

item.title: Cut PR costs from $80 to $20 not by switching models but by writing the factory as code

item.description: After defining its internal software factory entirely as code and wiring in an observability loop, Warp compressed PR costs from $80 to $15–20 through measure-and-optimize, while lifting PR throughput 40%.
item.content:encoded:
After defining its internal software factory entirely as code and wiring in an observability loop, Warp compressed PR costs from $80 to $15–20 through measure-and-optimize, while lifting PR throughput 40%.

Breaks down the layered technical stack a software factory needs, shows Warp's before/after real costs and throughput when tuning its agent system—numbers a team can benchmark against, not product talk.

2:03 Software factories aren't built by bolting automation together
Zach argues that most companies calling themselves a software factory have simply added some agent-assisted coding—a fundamental misunderstanding. His definition: a cloud-hosted agentic system where teams explicitly define agent roles in the build process, the system exercises autonomy, is measurable and benchmarkable, forms a closed loop, and can be tuned over time to build confidence. That's categorically different from ad-hoc automation.

4:10 The factory definition itself must run as code
Against the myth that "buy a tool and get a money machine," Zach insists the factory must be concrete and runnable. Define it in YAML: which repos, which MCP integrations, which skills. Write the entire workflow declaratively—like Terraform—so it versions, branches for testing, and rolls back on demand. That's the only way to escape loose automation fragments that can't be versioned or audited.

6:15 All agent work, wherever it starts, must feed one central system
Whether a task lands in Slack, Linear, or GitHub, it must enter the same system to trigger pre-defined workflows. Only then do you see the complete trace: computer-use screenshots, every orchestration detail, agent-to-agent handoffs. Most companies can't do this because engineers each run Cloud Code or Codex locally, data completely fragmented across laptops and logs.

14:36 Agents should submit pull requests to improve the factory code
Because the factory definition is code, Warp's self-improving agents analyze historical failures—they spotted 54 cases where the triage agent should have spawned sub-agents but didn't—then submit PRs directly to the factory definition to fix the workflow. It's a complete learning loop, though Zach admits they haven't yet replayed history to verify the fix actually works. That's the next-level capability being built now.

16:41 Real benchmarks must test model and harness combinations together
Zach argues you can't benchmark models in isolation; you must benchmark models and harness together. Warp runs the same real-world tasks with different model/harness combinations (Warp's own, Cloud Code, Codex, Pi), plots cost-versus-correctness curves, gets results for their specific business rather than generic leaderboards, then feeds those results into model/harness routing strategy.

23:51 Tuning can cut per-PR costs to one-quarter of starting point
Warp tuned its own system this way: started at ~$80 per PR (too much Opus, over-trained triage models, sub-agents split too finely); brought it down to $15–20. Month-over-month, PR throughput jumped 40% while revert rate stayed flat. Zach calls that the proof that observe-measure-optimize actually works—not just in theory but in the production cost structure of an agentic platform.

26:58 Teams smaller than five to ten engineers should not use this
Asked who really needs this platform, Zach draws a clear line: small teams just buy Cloud Code or Codex; this platform is overkill for them. The real breakeven is roughly 5–10 engineers and up. Bigger companies need it more, but deployment complexity grows with scale. Growth-stage companies at 10–100 people with Slack and Linear already in place can often self-serve.

31:07 When API costs are too high, small companies rotate subscriptions
On the hardest objection: some small companies desperately want this system but can't afford it, so they're cycling through $200 subscriptions to piece together capacity, because per-API billing runs 5–50 times more expensive than subscriptions. Zach admits he's unsure whether rotating subscriptions violates the service terms, but concedes it's currently the cheapest way—it just doesn't scale as a company grows.

item.title: Anthropic's bill makes it nearly impossible to halt dangerous AI training
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-eightythousand-anthropic的法案让人几乎没法叫停危险的ai训练/
item.description: The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.
item.content:encoded:
The bill compresses the power to halt training into a single Commerce Secretary signature and a single DC court decision within 45 days—when models actually cause harm, there's almost no time to hit the brakes.

A dense solo episode: the evidence chains and perspectives on three major scandals are laid out clearly and worth hearing in full.

1:34 Bill compresses authority to stop dangerous training through a dangerously narrow bottleneck
Under the federal AI bill that Anthropic privately championed, the only way to halt a model's training is for the Commerce Secretary to personally sign off and submit the case to a single federal court in Washington DC. The government must prove the risk is ‘imminent’, must prove lighter interventions won't work, and judges must review from scratch without deference to regulators. Any halt order expires automatically after 45 days; reauthorizing requires proving the case all over again. More critically, even whether ‘a 10% human extinction probability within the next year’counts as ‘imminent’ is undefined—and that gap determines whether this gate can actually block truly catastrophic risks.

4:02 CEO estimates 25% disaster probability, yet company strips halt authority
The contradiction: this bill comes from a company whose CEO publicly puts the probability of AI ‘causing major chaos’at 25% and has written that ‘recursive self-improvement must proceed with extreme care, if at all’. The host sees why—Anthropic has been in frequent conflict with the Trump administration this year and fears federal discretionary power will be weaponized for political concessions rather than genuinely controlling dangerous research. But he argues the solution shouldn't be stripping away state power too; instead preserve states like California's independent halt authority, or at least let state attorneys general petition the DC court as well. You shouldn't stake everything on one agency's review by a single court.

5:15 Bill would retroactively eliminate state-level AI safety laws nationwide
The bill not only narrows federal authority but also bars states from requiring AI companies to disclose safety plans, undergo independent audits, or report incidents—effectively retroactively nullifying flagship AI laws already passed in California, Illinois, and New York. There's a subtler provision: states had the power to halt models presenting ‘major catastrophic risk’using ‘statute, regulation, directive, court decision or other action’; under the bill's design, that power eventually disappears too. The result: even if California's government unanimously determined an unreleased model could kill everyone in the state, it would have no power to legislate or seek a court injunction—only hope the Commerce Secretary will run that process.

8:58 OpenAI fired three safety researchers on the same afternoon over disputed evidence
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang were each fired at a 2 p.m. meeting on the same afternoon, with contradictory and unpersuasive justifications. OpenAI later claimed the real reason was ‘broken trust’but refused to explain. According to reports, the trigger was a leak investigation: news had surfaced that OpenAI's new model used ‘looped transformer’technology, which the company wanted hidden. Investigators suspected the leak came via Signal messages between one researcher and outside contact Ryan Greenblatt, but both used disappearing messages—neither could prove innocence. Looped transformers let models perform hidden calculations before outputting chain-of-thought reasoning; the field has long warned this points toward unmonitorable models. All three researchers had previously publicly supported keeping chain-of-thought observable.

10:12 The evidence for firing the three was far weaker than stated
Disappearing messages are standard in tech and AI circles—you can't convict based on that alone, or everyone from CEO down would be suspect. The Information, which broke this story, has sourced OpenAI's internal secrets for years from investors, ex-employees, even casual conversation—not necessarily these three. Hundreds, possibly two hundred OpenAI employees could oppose looped transformers—this year alone, nearly 400 signed a petition demanding AI research slow for safety's sake. The host personally judges a Greenblatt leak highly unlikely; it doesn't fit his operating style at all. Conclusion: firing was probably error. The cost: the company will struggle to get candid employee input going forward, and the actual leaker may never be found.

12:52 Google DeepMind's contracts silence employees for life, not just at departure
According to BBC reporting, Google DeepMind's UK employment contracts forbid employees from publicly criticizing anything Google does—for life. The clause surfaced when a former employee tried to criticize Google's sale of AI to the US Defense Department (usable as long as DoD deems it legal), a deal that already prompted resignations over principle. This echoes the ‘non-disparagement agreement’scandal uncovered two years ago at OpenAI: former employees criticizing the company lost stock worth potentially tens of millions, and the clause itself demanded secrecy. After exposure, both OpenAI and Anthropic admitted to similar clauses and promised to drop them. Google DeepMind's version has no secrecy requirement and doesn't forfeit stock, but the lawsuit threat alone creates massive chilling effect on ordinary employees.

17:31 Speaking up inside requires public channels; speaking out requires going public
The host offers a graduated approach: to stay, calmly and rationally explain specific reasons for opposing a decision in public Slack channels colleagues will see, focusing on the few most critical points, not opposing everything reflexively, and staying open to being persuaded. If reasonable dissent gets no satisfactory response, escalate to publicly stating this makes you question the company's judgment and strategy—and that you're considering leaving. Still no results: submit a thorough resignation statement, then make your case public after departure. His reasoning: companies automate employee work faster by the year, so employees' bargaining power erodes over time. ‘If not now, when?’

21:39 Outside pressure reshapes corporate governance when insiders organize the pressure
Against OpenAI's plan to hollow out its nonprofit parent and charitable mission, the ‘Not For Private Gain’campaign had few participants but, paired with state attorneys general attention and broader coalition pressure, forced OpenAI to substantially revise: the OpenAI Foundation gained approximately 75 billion dollars in additional equity, and its Safety & Alignment Committee locked down decision rights over a range of safety questions. Similar: a 2024 campaign by former employees for ‘right to raise concerns’that became whistleblower protections in California's SB 53; continued reporting showing OpenAI publicly backing regulation while lobbying against it also pushed OpenAI to support SB 53-type rules and led President Greg Brockman to stop giving to the lobbying PAC ‘Leading the Future’.

item.title: Your A-share losses come from understanding that can't keep pace with change
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-touzishizhan-亏钱不是a股的错-是你对它的认知不够/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-touzishizhan-亏钱不是a股的错-是你对它的认知不够/
item.description: After reviewing his 60+-percent drawdown this year, Zhang Jun discovered that the root cause of A-shares' short bull runs and long bear markets—and investors' short time horizons—was never the market itself, but investors' understanding of intrinsic value and macroeconomic cycles failing to keep pace with change's speed.
item.content:encoded:
After reviewing his 60+-percent drawdown this year, Zhang Jun discovered that the root cause of A-shares' short bull runs and long bear markets—and investors' short time horizons—was never the market itself, but investors' understanding of intrinsic value and macroeconomic cycles failing to keep pace with change's speed.

An honest retrospective from a fund manager running private equity for years after a major drawdown, from rereading Graham's original work to the storage-chip case—information-dense.

4:09 The index barely moved, but whole sectors were sliced in half
Zhang Jun highlights a counterintuitive fact: Shanghai Composite's full-year range was under 20 percent, from January highs above 4,200 to lows above 3,600. Yet beneath that, sub-indices swung wildly. ChiNext and STAR Board each fell roughly 40 percent from June peaks; the optical module index dropped over 50 percent from its high. His point: concentrated sector bets faced far steeper drawdowns than the aggregate index suggests.

5:09 Even dividend low-volatility funds got turned into high-volatility assets
Zhang Jun adds that supposedly defensive dividend plays didn't escape the carnage: the baijiu index fell 30-odd percent on its worst days; the dividend low-volatility index—promised stability—was down 10 points in its worst month. More tragicomically, in June when the market rallied and tech soared, this index fell 10 points in a single month, then gained them back in July when the market fell—behaving the exact opposite of its name.

12:12 Every industry has its own Xu Jiayin
Zhang Jun argues Chinese firms cannot sustain stable EPS growth because of abundant ‘entrepreneurial ambition’: CEOs want to expand scale, CFOs and key technologists push expansion and capex to advance their careers, and local governments' investment drives force companies to boost capital spending. Everyone knows Xu Jiayin, he notes, but every industry has its own version—the property sector's just leveraged hard enough to crater publicly.

20:14 Graham never said to discount future cash flows
Zhang Jun revisits years of misreading Graham: value investors picture DCF models calculating intrinsic value, but that was Williams' idea, not Graham's. In “Security Analysis”, Graham calculated working capital and net asset discounts—the goal was finding a margin of safety, not pinning an exact intrinsic value number. He restates Graham's actual logic in three sentences: stocks are stakes in businesses; Mr. Market is a quotation device to exploit; and margins of safety matter.

22:15 Intrinsic value isn't a point—it's a moving range
He cites a cutting-tool stock he sold too early this year: bought at 2 billion+ market cap aiming for 10 billion in three years, but AI-driven M&A turbocharged earnings to target, so he sold per plan—only later discovering the company's intrinsic value was still climbing fast and he'd treated a dynamic company as static. Takeaway: intrinsic value is never a fixed point but a range that shifts up and down with fundamentals; exit timing should track that range's velocity.

31:22 Storage chip prices spike, but intrinsic value may not follow
When asked whether ‘rising demand equals rising intrinsic value,’ Zhang Jun uses storage chips to refute the simple narrative: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron learned overexpansion's sting, intentionally restrained supply to barely maintain a three-player oligopoly—then AI sent prices skyward, but now they're expanding again while YMTC enters. His conclusion: once a carefully guarded competitive structure cracks, surface price rallies and demand figures don't simply equal long-term intrinsic-value gains.

35:25 Whether to add on dips—the question itself is the answer
Facing scenarios where stock price falls below your entry but intrinsic value falls faster (so margin of safety looks bigger), Zhang Jun offers this heuristic: if you're asking friends whether to add to a losing position, that act alone proves you don't understand it well enough—sell immediately. As long as intrinsic value is still sliding and you can't find new evidence of a bottom, buying purely because the price is low is short-term gambling and probably catching a knife mid-fall.

50:42 Value investors with sweeping sector coverage—I'm skeptical
Zhang Jun offers an ‘immature observation’: no one can be expert in packaged food, consumer electronics, and AI simultaneously. If someone calling themselves a value investor covers too many industries, he doubts their authenticity. He reviews his own past expansion into chemicals, pharma, information security, and solar—convinced at the time he was applying value-investing method, but in hindsight nearly every call was wrong. Example: pharma volume-based pricing policy disruptions happened long before he grasped that industry logic had shifted.

item.title: Next fiscal year, Nvidia must finance a quarter of its own revenue
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-laoshi-下一财年-英伟达四分之一营收要靠自己给客户撑腰/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-03-laoshi-下一财年-英伟达四分之一营收要靠自己给客户撑腰/
item.description: Nvidia packages GPUs as financeable assets while funding AI labs and extending credit to customers buying its chips, propping up revenue through circular financing and driving accounts receivable to $63.1 billion.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia packages GPUs as financeable assets while funding AI labs and extending credit to customers buying its chips, propping up revenue through circular financing and driving accounts receivable to $63.1 billion.

Complete breakdown of Nvidia's production, capital, and industrial strategy at three levels; circular financing and accounts receivable are most valuable for assessing whether AI infrastructure is overheating.

1:02 Computing power is revenue—Jevons Paradox means cheaper chips drive volume growth
Huang has inverted the old accounting. GPUs were once an expense to minimize; now they're production assets that generate returns. But his wager rests on Jevons Paradox: as compute gets cheaper, the surge in demand activates new use cases—contract reviews, email, simulation—that were economically unviable before. Volume must grow fast enough to offset falling prices. If it does, Nvidia widens margins despite cheaper chips.

4:02 AI agents never sleep—they parallelize and multiply compute demand by orders of magnitude
Agents differ from humans: they reason, plan, call tools, iterate repeatedly, work without sleeping or procrastinating, and can spawn hundreds of copies running in parallel. An engineer might manually run dozens of simulations a day; an agent can generate thousands of parameter combinations and optimize them autonomously. Human software interactions are dropping while background compute demand explodes. Agents don't just need GPU—they need CPU for scheduling, memory and storage for state, networking to connect tools and systems. One machine's gains lift everything around it.

5:03 Tokens are intermediate products; value is solving problems correctly, not token count
A steel mill produces a ton of steel, sells it, makes cash. An AI factory produces ten million tokens that might be worth nothing. An agent might spin for an hour burning millions of tokens to fix a bug, only to make the code worse, forcing engineers to spend extra time cleaning up the mess. Nvidia cares about tokens-per-watt and tokens-per-dollar. Users care about spending money to solve one thing correctly. When they align, everyone wins. When algorithm innovation lets models use fewer tokens for the same task, that's good for users—but not necessarily for vendors selling hardware by token throughput.

7:03 Per gigawatt, Nvidia captures revenue from $18 billion to $40 billion across chip generations
The AI factory's total efficiency—not a single GPU—determines pricing power. By Nvidia's own math, for each gigawatt of power a customer receives, the device-purchase revenue flowing to Nvidia was approximately $18 billion in the Hopper era, $25 billion in Blackwell, and $40 billion in the Vera Rubin generation. That extra money isn't higher GPU prices. It's that Nvidia has more to sell: networking, software, the full stack ecosystem. Even if customers use competitors' GPUs or custom silicon, networking and systems still flow through Nvidia. It keeps collecting rent.

8:03 DSXPORT cuts data center deployment from six months to as little as two weeks
DSXPORT pre-assembles entire AI factories in modular containers—racks, wiring, liquid cooling, system validation—all done in the factory. At the site, power, cooling, and networking just need to be ready. Deployment time drops from six months to as little as fourteen days. Huang's calculation: an AI factory generates $40 billion annually in revenue; three months of delay is tens of billions in sunk loss. But gross margins on infrastructure components don't match GPU margins, and this quarter's 75% overall gross margin may face seasonal pressure ahead.

13:08 Circular financing inflates revenue while extending credit disguised as long payment terms
Nvidia's management keeps repeating three words—productive, fungible, durable—to convince Wall Street that GPUs are stable, long-term, resellable assets. Customers can then use equipment as loan collateral. Nvidia itself invests heavily: supply and capacity commitments now exceed $279 billion, plus nearly $50 billion into AI labs. This quarter's $96.2 billion revenue grew 106% year-over-year. Yet accounts receivable hit $63.1 billion with collection periods around sixty days. More revenue isn't real cash. It's extended as long payment terms, accounting entries sitting with customers. Nvidia is using its own balance sheet to funnel hidden loans.

17:10 Every AI strategy—U.S., China, Europe—must pay Nvidia's infrastructure toll regardless of approach
The U.S. pursues frontier models plus high-value services; the challenge is whether billion-dollar investments pay back and custom chips reduce Nvidia reliance. China pursues open ecosystems and extreme engineering efficiency; DeepSeek and other open models lower the barrier to entry, paired with manufacturing-sector AI deployment; the challenge is competing under compute constraints. Europe pursues industrial applications and sovereign AI—adapting open models to local industrial data for domain-specific training. The earnings report signals the outcome: ACIE customers (non-hyperscaler data centers) contributed roughly $40 billion, up 138% year-over-year, outpacing overall data-center growth. Every path requires paying Nvidia's toll.

19:14 Nvidia's model survives only if three conditions hold: productivity gains, capital access, market share
Three balance sheets determine how long Huang's economics last. The technology account asks: does AI actually raise productivity, or does it stop at keynote demos? The capital account asks: is AI infrastructure expansion funded by customer subscriptions or increasingly by Wall Street financing and Nvidia's own balance sheet propping it up? Circular financing that re-invests its own returns is a snowball that eventually needs an accounting. The industry account asks: after markets mature, will open models and application companies capture a larger slice? Huang's historical reminder: the biggest winner in a technological revolution isn't always whoever solved the infrastructure bottleneck first.
